section_1.title: Prerequisite Warm-up: The Basis Vectors
section_1.content: Briefly revisit 3D space defined by standard basis vectors i(1,0,0), j(0,1,0), and k(0,0,1). Explain that a linear transformation is simply where these basis vectors land after a transformation.
section_1.example: Imagine three unit-length arrows (axes) anchored at the origin; watch how they move to new positions in 3D space.

section_2.title: The Transformation Matrix
section_2.content: Introduce the 3x3 matrix as a storage container for the new coordinates of i, j, and k. Column 1 is the new i, Column 2 the new j, and Column 3 the new k.
section_2.example: Representing a scaling transformation where the x-axis doubles, y-axis stays, and z-axis triples using a diagonal matrix: diag(2, 1, 3).

section_3.title: Visualizing Transformations: Shear and Rotation
section_3.content: Demonstrate that linear transformations keep the origin fixed and grid lines parallel. Introduce 3D rotation (e.g., around the z-axis) and shearing (slanting a cube into a parallelepiped).
section_3.example: Visualizing a 'Robot Arm' joint rotating a 3D block, or a stack of cards being 'sheared' into a tilted shape.

section_4.title: Determinants and Volume Scaling
section_4.content: Explain the geometric meaning of the determinant of a 3x3 matrix: it represents the factor by which the transformation scales the volume of any shape.
section_4.example: If a unit cube with volume 1 transforms into a parallelepiped with volume 2, the absolute value of the determinant of the transformation matrix is 2.

section_5.title: Real-world Application: Computer Graphics
section_5.content: Synthesize knowledge by showing how matrices are chained to move complex 3D models in games or engineering software.
section_5.example: A 3D character (e.g., a rabbit) being rotated and scaled in a game engine; each frame is just the result of a sequence of matrix-vector multiplications.
